cards.h: The most famous animal in physics
cards.b: Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat in 1935 to show how absurd it seems if quantum rules are stretched to everyday things. Today the question it raises, why we do not see everyday superpositions, has a partial answer called decoherence, and it is the biggest obstacle for building quantum computers.

A cat sits in a sealed box with a vial of poison that is released if one radioactive atom decays. The atom is in a superposition of "decayed" and "not decayed" until observed. If quantum rules apply all the way up, the cat is a superposition of alive and dead.

Schrödinger did not think this was true. He meant it as a challenge: the theory, taken literally, seems silly at large scales. It was a thought experiment; no one has put a cat in a box this way.

The theory has no built-in size limit. Yet we never see a cat, a chair or a cricket ball in a blend of two places. Either the rules change at some size, or something else hides the quantum behaviour. Different interpretations pick different answers (previous lesson).

A real system is never alone. A dust grain is bombarded by air molecules and light. Each tiny contact records a little information about where the grain is. That information, scattered into the environment, is the same as "watching" in the double-slit experiment: the stripes disappear.

H. Dieter Zeh (1970) and Wojciech Zurek (from 1981) developed this idea. The coherence needed for interference leaks away into countless environment particles.

A drop of ink in a bucket swirls into patterns you could in principle reverse. Dropped into a river, the ink spreads so widely it is lost for ever in practice.

Where it breaks: in decoherence the information is not destroyed, only spread out. Strictly, the whole thing plus environment is still a superposition.

It explains

Why everyday objects look classical, why the stripes vanish, how fast the quantum look fades (extremely fast for big warm things).

It does not explain

Why you see one outcome. After decoherence the mix looks like "either this or that", but you still need an interpretation (many-worlds, collapse, pilot wave) to say why one happens.

• Serge Haroche (Paris, 1996): atoms in a cavity made tiny "Schrödinger kitten" states, and watched them decohere in milliseconds. Haroche and David Wineland shared the 2012 Nobel.
  • Arndt, Zeilinger and others: heating C60 molecules makes them radiate and the stripes fade, as predicted.
  • 2025 Nobel (Clarke, Devoret, Martinis): quantum behaviour in a large circuit.
  • Quantum computers: engineers fight decoherence daily; qubits last microseconds to milliseconds in superconducting devices.

• "The cat is both dead and alive." By decoherence, within a fraction of a second the box is not in a sharp blend; what remains is the interpretation question.
  • "A conscious observer is needed." A cat counts as an environment, and so does a stray photon.
  • "Decoherence solves the measurement problem." Not alone.

E.C.G. Sudarshan is a co-author (with Gorini and Kossakowski, 1976) of the GKSL equation (also called Lindblad), the standard mathematical description of how a quantum system loses coherence. It is used by every quantum computing group worldwide, including the labs at TIFR and IISc under the National Quantum Mission.

• Schrödinger's cat (1935) was a challenge to stretching quantum rules to big objects.
  • Decoherence (Zeh, Zurek) explains why big warm things look classical.
  • It hides the blend but does not by itself say why one outcome occurs.

Think about it

  1. Why does a cold, isolated atom stay quantum longer than a warm cat?
  2. Why is decoherence the main enemy of quantum computers?

quiz.w: As a challenge to naive quantum extrapolation.

quiz.q: What was the cat meant to show?
o: Quantum rules look absurd if applied to everyday objects
Loss of quantum interference by interaction with the environment

quiz.q: Why do big warm objects decohere fast?
o: They are not made of atoms
quiz.w: Air, light and heat constantly record them.

quiz.q: Does decoherence alone explain why we see one outcome?
o: No, an interpretation is still needed
quiz.w: It removes interference but not the choice.
